html:
The Late and Final Jōmon were the last stages of Japan's long Jōmon culture, from about 2500 to 300 BCE. The map shows the label from 1500 to 400 BCE.

Jōmon people were hunters, fishers and gatherers who made some of the world's oldest pottery and lived in settled villages for thousands of years. By the Late Jōmon a cooler climate had cut the population of eastern Japan well below its peak. People moved toward the coasts and lived more from the sea, leaving large shell mounds.

Ritual seems to have grown. Northern Japan has stone circles from this time, and potters made clay figurines, dogū, some with goggle eyes, as well as fine lacquered pottery in the Final Jōmon style of the northeast.

Sometime around 1000 to 800 BCE wet rice farming arrived in northern Kyushu from the Korean Peninsula, and the Yayoi culture spread east. In the far north the old way of life lasted much longer and leads toward the Ainu.
